how-to-use-lip-scrub.before:
Dry, flaky lips are one of the first things cold weather, central heating and long days in a mask or scarf leave behind. A lip scrub lifts the loose, flaky bits so your lips feel smooth again, and a good lip balm straight after keeps them soft. Here is how to use a lip scrub, how often, and which lip balm to pair with it.

What is a lip scrub?

A lip scrub is a small pot of fine sugar held in butters and oils. The sugar does the gentle polishing; the butters and oils leave a soft, cushioned layer behind. Ours are short, simple blends:

  • Deyga Mint Lip Scrub (£12.99, 16g): avocado and almond oils, beeswax, shea butter, granulated sugar, mint essential oil and vitamin E. Fresh and cooling to use.
  • Deyga Strawberry Lip Scrub (£10.99, 16g): the same base with strawberry essential oil for a fruity scent, free from artificial colours, alcohol and parabens.
  • Vilvah Natural Lip Scrub (£6.99, 10g): organic shea butter, avocado and almond oils, organic sugar, beeswax, and lemon and spearmint essential oils, free from alcohol and silicones. The small pot is easy to keep in a handbag.

How to use a lip scrub

  1. Start with clean, dry lips. Take off lipstick or balm first.
  2. Take a small amount, about the size of a grain of rice, on a clean fingertip.
  3. Massage in small circles for 30 seconds to a minute. Use light pressure: let the sugar do the work.
  4. Wipe or rinse it off with a soft, damp cloth or lukewarm water. Some people simply lick the sugar away.
  5. Apply a lip balm straight away, while lips are soft and smooth.

How often should you use a lip scrub?

For most people, two or three times a week is plenty. Lip skin is thin, so scrubbing every day can leave it feeling sore. In winter, or if your lips are very dry, use it when they feel flaky rather than on a fixed schedule. Before a matte or long-wear lipstick, a quick scrub helps the colour go on more evenly.

The lip balm to follow it

A scrub without a balm is only half the job. Choose the balm by what you want from it.

A natural lip balm for everyday

Deyga Beetroot Lip Balm Classic (from £10.99, 10g) blends beetroot extract with almond, avocado and jojoba oils, shea butter, beeswax and vitamin E. The beetroot gives lips a soft, natural flush. Deyga Natural Lip Balm (£9.99, 8g) is the plain choice: almond and jojoba oils, beeswax, shea butter and vanilla extract, in a light, non-greasy texture that sits well under lipstick.

A tinted lip balm

If you like a hint of colour, the Deyga Beetroot Lip Balm Stick (from £13.99, 5.5g) has the same beetroot blend in an easy tube. Vilvah Grape Fruit Lip Balm (£6.99) adds red iron oxide for a tint, with organic shea butter, avocado and almond oils and grapefruit essential oil. The Vilvah Tinted Lip Balm Kit (£17.99) brings two tinted balms together.

An SPF lip balm for daytime

Lips burn too, and most lip balms have no sun protection. Vilvah Milk Lip Balm SPF 30 PA+++ (£9.99) uses mineral filters, titanium dioxide and zinc oxide, with soy milk, soy butter, shea butter and kokum butter. Wear it outdoors and reapply as the pack directs, especially after eating or drinking.

A rich lip butter for night

Highborn London Superior Lip Butter (£22.50, 15ml) is a richer, softer texture to smooth on before bed after a scrub.

Lip scrub and balm sets

Sets pair a scrub with its balm, and make a neat small gift or stocking filler:

  • Deyga Soft Lip Combo (£17.99): Mint Lip Scrub and Beetroot Lip Balm.
  • Deyga Nourished Lip Care Kit (£25.99): Strawberry Lip Scrub and Beetroot Lip Balm.
  • Vilvah Lip Nourishing Kit (£13.99): Vilvah Lip Scrub and Grapefruit Lip Balm.

For more small gifts, see our Christmas gift guide.

Part of a wider routine

Lips are the driest skin of all, but the same idea works for the body: polish, then moisturise. Read how to choose a body scrub and how to use a body butter. Not sure which natural brand to start with? Compare them in Deyga or Vilvah.

Good to know

  • Patch test first, especially with scrubs and balms that contain essential oils such as mint, lemon or grapefruit.
  • Skip the scrub on cracked, cut, sore or sunburnt lips, or during a cold sore. Use only a balm until they have settled.
  • Lips that stay sore, split or swollen for a long time are worth showing to a pharmacist or your GP.
  • Keep pots clean: use a clean fingertip and close the lid after use.

natural-shampoo-guide.before:
More people are switching to a natural shampoo: one built on plant-derived cleansers, with milks, waters and botanical extracts in place of a long list of synthetics. But "natural" is not a legal term in the UK, so the label alone tells you little. Here is how to read a shampoo, which one suits dry hair, frizz or a flaky scalp, and the conditioner or hair mask to follow it with.

What makes a shampoo "natural"?

Every shampoo needs a cleanser to lift oil and dirt. In the shampoos below, most come from coconut, corn or sugar beet: names such as decyl glucoside, coco-glucoside, sodium cocoyl isethionate and cocamidopropyl betaine. Around them sit the ingredients that give each shampoo its character, such as rice water, goat milk, rosemary or neem. Always read the full ingredient list on the product page: it tells you far more than the word "natural" on the front.

Shampoo for dry hair

Dry hair needs a cleanse that leaves moisture behind. Look for a creamy shampoo with milks, proteins or oils.

  • Vilvah Goat Milk Shampoo (£15.99, 250ml): goat milk and jasmine flower water with hydrolysed keratin, pea protein, panthenol and jojoba oil, in a creamy lather. Vilvah makes it for dry, frizzy or chemically treated hair.
  • Deyga Rice Water Shampoo (from £10.99, 50ml or 220ml): rice water with coconut- and corn-derived cleansers. A light, everyday shampoo for all hair types.

Rice water shampoo

Rice water has long been used in Asian hair care, where people rinsed their hair with the water left from soaking rice. A rice water shampoo puts that into an easy, everyday cleanser; the Deyga one leads its ingredient list with rice water and leaves hair feeling soft and smooth.

Shampoo for a flaky scalp

Scalp shampoos use herbal ingredients with a fresh, clean feel:

  • Vilvah Herbal Shampoo for Dandruff Control (from £12.99): neem leaf, tea tree and black pepper oils, rosemary and basil waters and amla, made without parabens.
  • Deyga Anti Dandruff Shampoo (£14.99, 220ml): rosemary leaf hydrosol, ginger extract and a yeast ferment extract, with mild cleansers. Deyga makes it for frequent use and says it is safe for colour-treated hair.

Massage it into the scalp, not just the lengths, and leave it for a minute before rinsing. Flakes, itching or redness that do not settle are worth showing to a pharmacist or your GP. Shop every shampoo for dandruff, or see our dandruff care edit.

Conditioner for dry hair

Conditioner smooths the hair after shampoo, so it detangles easily and feels softer.

  • Vilvah Cream Conditioner (£15.99, 250ml): tucuma butter, broccoli seed oil, aloe vera, jasmine and pea protein. Vilvah says it can also be left on for up to 15 minutes as a mask.
  • Deyga Soy Milk Conditioner (£11.99, 50ml): soybean extract, argan oil, provitamin B5 and vitamin E in a lightweight texture.

Hair mask for dry hair

Once a week, swap your conditioner for a mask. Vilvah Goat Milk Hair Mask (£31.99, 200g) combines goat milk with ceramides, argan oil, vitamin E and a seaweed extract. Apply it to clean, damp lengths, leave it for 10 to 15 minutes, then rinse. Vilvah says it also works as a leave-in styling aid for curls. See every hair mask for dry hair.

How to wash your hair

  1. Wet your hair thoroughly with warm, not hot, water.
  2. Use a coin-sized amount of shampoo, more for long or thick hair.
  3. Focus on the scalp, massaging with your fingertips, not your nails. The lather will clean the lengths as you rinse.
  4. Rinse well, then apply conditioner to the mid-lengths and ends.
  5. Leave it for a minute or two, comb through with a wide-tooth comb, and rinse.
  6. Pat dry with a towel rather than rubbing, which can rough up the hair.

How often? Dry or curly hair often does well with two or three washes a week; an oily scalp may prefer every other day. Natural shampoos can lather less than you are used to, so a second, smaller wash is fine.

Before and after the wash

Oiling before a wash is a long tradition in Indian hair care: read our guide to hair oils. For frizz after drying, a few drops of serum help smooth flyaways; the Vilvah Shampoo & Hair Serum Kit (£25.99) pairs the Goat Milk Shampoo with the Anti-Frizz Hair Serum. See all hair serums for frizzy hair.

Good to know

  • Patch test a new shampoo behind the ear, especially one with essential oils such as tea tree or rosemary.
  • Keep it out of your eyes; rinse with water if it gets in.
  • Switching brands? Give your hair two or three weeks to settle before you judge.

deyga-or-vilvah.before:
If you are looking for natural skincare in the UK with roots in Indian beauty traditions, two names come up again and again: Deyga and Vilvah. Both are Indian brands, both work with plant-based and kitchen-cupboard ingredients, and Swansura is an official UK partner of both, so every product is genuine and ships from the UK. They are not the same, though. Here is how to tell which one suits your skin, and where to start.

The short answer

Choose Vilvah if you like creamy, comforting textures built around goat milk, oat milk and gentle botanicals. Choose Deyga if you prefer farm-grown herbs, clays, charcoal and fruit actives with a fresher feel. Many people end up using both: a Vilvah cleanser or serum in the morning and a Deyga treat, such as a lip balm or face pack, alongside it.

Vilvah: goat milk and botanical care

Vilvah is known for milk-based formulas for face, hair and body. The best place to start is Vilvah Milk Drops Hydrating Serum, a lightweight milk serum with natural milk proteins that sinks in quickly and leaves skin feeling soft rather than greasy. It is the product people search for most: "Vilvah Milk Drops" is one of the brand's top searches in the UK.

For hair, the Vilvah Goat Milk Shampoo pairs goat milk with pea protein and jasmine. In India, oiling your hair is a weekly ritual passed down through families: warm oil massaged into the scalp, left to soak in, then washed out. It is one of the simplest ways to make dry hair feel softer and look glossier, and it is easy to start. Here is what the classic ingredients (amla, bhringraj, castor oil and more) bring to a hair oil, how to choose one, and how to oil your hair step by step.

What does a hair oil do?

A hair oil coats the hair shaft, so lengths feel softer, smoother and less frizzy, and look shinier. Used before washing, it cushions the lengths so they feel less dry after shampoo. And the scalp massage that goes with it is relaxing in itself. Think of a hair oil as a conditioning treatment for hair and scalp.

The key ingredients, explained

  • Amla (Indian gooseberry, Emblica officinalis) is the best-known ingredient in Ayurvedic hair care. In an amla hair oil, the dried fruit is steeped in a base oil such as coconut.
  • Bhringraj (Eclipta prostrata) is a herb traditionally used in Indian hair oils, often alongside amla. Bhringraj oil is usually a herbal infusion rather than a pure oil.
  • Castor oil is thick and rich. On its own it can feel heavy, so it works best mixed with lighter oils, which is how you will find it in most blends.
  • Coconut oil is the classic base for Indian hair oils, light enough for the scalp and rich enough for the lengths.
  • Hibiscus, fenugreek and curry leaf are kitchen-garden ingredients that often join amla in traditional blends.
  • Neem, tea tree and peppermint give an oil a fresh, cooling feel on the scalp.
  • Rosemary essential oil adds a herbal scent and is a popular addition to modern blends.

Our hair oils, compared

  • Deyga Hair Growth Oil (£14.99, 100ml): virgin coconut, almond, castor and sunflower oils infused with amla, bhringraj, hibiscus, fenugreek, curry leaves and other herbs, plus rosemary essential oil. A lightweight blend with an applicator tip for the scalp, and free from mineral oil and synthetic fragrance.
  • Vilvah Hair Growth Oil (£31.99, 200ml): pumpkin seed, black seed (kalonji), castor, grapeseed and almond oils with vitamin E, rosemary and peppermint. Alcohol-free and non-sticky.
  • Deyga Premature Greying Hair Oil (£18.99, 100ml): virgin coconut oil infused with amla, bhringraj, henna, bakuchi, moringa and liquorice, a classic Ayurvedic herbal blend.
  • Vilvah Anti-Dandruff Hair Oil (£19.99, 100ml): almond, neem and sesame oils with tea tree, peppermint, camphor, lemon and basil oils and amla oil, for a fresh, cooling scalp massage.
  • Deyga Neem Seed Oil (£14.99, 30ml): pure cold-pressed neem seed oil, a single ingredient. It has a strong natural smell, so most people mix a few drops into a lighter oil.

See every hair oil in one place.

A note on "hair growth" oils

Hair growth oil is one of the most searched hair care terms in the UK, and it is the name several brands give their blends (see them on our hair growth oil page). Be realistic about what any oil can do: it conditions hair and scalp, makes lengths feel softer and helps them look healthier. Hair loss has many causes, from genes to hormones, stress and diet, and no oil can change those. If you notice sudden, patchy or heavy hair loss, speak to your GP.

How to oil your hair, step by step

  1. Start with dry or slightly damp hair, before you wash it.
  2. Warm the oil. Stand the bottle in a bowl of warm water for a few minutes. Coconut-based oils turn solid in a cold bathroom; this melts them again.
  3. Part your hair into sections and apply a little oil along each parting with your fingertips or the applicator.
  4. Massage your scalp for 3 to 5 minutes with your fingertips in small circles, gently, without scratching.
  5. Smooth what is left through the lengths and ends, then comb through with a wide-tooth comb, such as a neem wood comb (£13.99).
  6. Leave it on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight with a towel over your pillow.
  7. Shampoo, and if hair still feels oily, shampoo a second time. Then condition the lengths.

Once or twice a week is plenty for most people.

Hair oil for dry hair

If your hair is dry, focus on the lengths and ends rather than the scalp, and choose a richer blend with coconut and castor oil. Between washes, smooth a single drop over the ends to tame flyaways, or use a lighter leave-in such as Vilvah Anti-Frizz Hair Serum (£28.99). More ideas: hair oil for dry hair and hair serum for frizzy hair.

Washing it out

A gentle shampoo removes oil without leaving hair squeaky and dry. Try Deyga Rice Water Shampoo (from £10.99) or Vilvah Goat Milk Shampoo (£15.99, 250ml) with goat milk, jasmine and pea protein. If your scalp tends to flake, Vilvah Herbal Shampoo for Dandruff Control (from £12.99) pairs with the Anti-Dandruff Hair Oil; see all shampoos for dandruff. If flaking or itching does not settle, ask a pharmacist. For more on choosing a shampoo, read our natural shampoo guide.

Good to know

  • Patch test first, especially with oils that contain essential oils such as tea tree, peppermint, camphor or rosemary.
  • Keep oil away from your eyes, and do not use it on a broken, sore or irritated scalp.
  • Protect your pillow and clothes: oils can mark fabric.

goat-milk-soap-guide.before:
Goat milk soap is a bar soap made with goat milk in its recipe. It gives a creamy lather and leaves skin feeling soft rather than tight, which is why many people keep a bar by the bath or basin. This guide explains how goat milk soap is made, how to use it on your face and body, and how to choose between the goat milk soaps from Vilvah, one of the two Indian natural brands Swansura is an official UK partner of.

What is goat milk soap?

Every true bar soap is made by mixing oils or butters with lye (sodium hydroxide). The two react together to form soap, a process called saponification. In goat milk soap, fresh goat milk goes into the recipe, which gives the bar a creamy lather. You will see sodium hydroxide at the end of the ingredient lists below: that is how all bar soap is made.

Vilvah makes its goat milk bars by hand with farm-fresh goat milk and a base of plant oils such as extra virgin olive, coconut and castor oil. Coconut oil gives the bubbly lather, olive oil a gentle feel and castor oil a cushioned foam.

The Vilvah goat milk soaps

  • Classic Goat Milk Soap (£9.99, 115g): goat milk, olive, coconut and castor oils, lightly scented with lavender essential oil. Six ingredients in all, and listed as suiting dry and sensitive skin.
  • Classic Rose Goat Milk Soap (£9.99, 125g): goat milk with rose petals, rose hydrosol, French pink clay, shea butter and rice bran oil, scented with rose and geranium essential oils.
  • Charcoal Goat Milk Soap (£9.99, 115g): activated charcoal with goat milk, for a clean-feeling daily wash. The charcoal gives the bar its colour.

All three are in our goat milk soap collection. One bar that looks similar is not a goat milk soap: Vilvah’s Cucumber, Curd & Mint Soap (£9.99) is made with cucumber juice, curd and mint leaves, for a cool, zesty morning wash.

Which bar should you choose?

  • A soft, simple scent: the Classic bar, with lavender.
  • A floral scent: Classic Rose.
  • A clean-feeling wash: Charcoal.
  • Something fresh and minty: Cucumber, Curd & Mint.
  • A bar without milk: Deyga’s Shea Saffron Bath Bar (£15.99) and Rose Pink Clay Bath Bar (£14.99) are made with raw shea butter and coconut and olive oils.

How to use goat milk soap

  1. Wet your skin and the bar, then work up a lather between your hands.
  2. Massage the foam over damp face or body, keeping it away from your eyes.
  3. Rinse well with warm water and pat dry.
  4. Follow with a moisturiser or body lotion if your skin tends to feel dry.
  5. Keep the bar on a draining soap dish between uses. A handmade bar left sitting in water softens quickly.

The Classic, Classic Rose and Cucumber bars contain essential oils, so patch test before first use.

Goat milk shampoo and hair care

Goat milk is not only for soap. Vilvah Goat Milk Shampoo (£15.99, 250ml) is a creamy shampoo with goat milk, jasmine flower water and hydrolysed pea protein, with a light jasmine and citrus scent. Vilvah Goat Milk Hair Mask (£31.99) pairs goat milk with ceramides and argan oil to condition dry, frizzy lengths. Buy them together in the Goat Milk Hair Kit (£34.99), or try the shampoo with Vilvah’s Cream Conditioner in the Bestseller Hair Kit (£27.99). Our natural shampoo guide covers how to choose a shampoo for dry hair.

Goat milk for the body

The Vilvah Milk Body Kit (£44.99) pairs a Goat Milk Body Wash, made with goat milk, chamomile water and coconut oil and scented with vanilla, with a Milk Body Lotion. If you were looking for a goat milk body lotion, note that the Milk Body Lotion (£25.99) is made with oat milk, ceramide NP and olive squalane: the goat milk in this kit is in the body wash. For richer body care after a soap, read our body butter guide.

  • Every skin is different. If you have a skin condition, ask a pharmacist or GP before trying a new soap.

Turmeric (haldi)

Turmeric is part of the Indian haldi ceremony before a wedding, when a turmeric paste is spread on the bride and groom. Neem

Neem is a tree grown across India, and its leaves and seeds are used in hair and skin care. Deyga Neem Seed Oil (£14.99) has one ingredient: neem seed oil, with a strong, earthy scent. Rose water (gulab jal)
